entities.name: Margaret Stewart, Dauphine of France
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Margaret Stewart (1424–1445), Dauphine of France, was a pivotal figure in the complex Anglo-French-Scottish diplomatic landscape of the mid-15th century, embodying a strategic alliance designed to counter English ambitions during the Hundred Years' War. As the eldest child of James I of Scotland and Joan Beaufort, her marriage to Louis XI, the future King of France, cemented the 'Auld Alliance,' a long-standing military and political pact between Scotland and France. Her brief but significant life illustrates the dynastic maneuvering and personal sacrifices inherent in medieval statecraft, connecting the royal houses of Stewart and Valois at a critical juncture for both kingdoms.

Born in Perth, Scotland, Margaret was betrothed to Louis, the eldest son of Charles VII of France, at the tender age of two, a testament to the urgency of the Anglo-French conflict. The marriage treaty, signed in 1428, stipulated a substantial dowry and military aid from Scotland. She embarked for France in 1436 at the age of 11, enduring a perilous sea voyage to escape English interception, and was formally married to the Dauphin Louis in Tours on June 25, 1436. Her life at the French court, particularly at Chinon and later at Châlons-en-Champagne, was reportedly marked by intellectual pursuits, including poetry, and a difficult relationship with her husband, who was reportedly cold and neglectful. Her delicate health and melancholic temperament were often attributed to the strains of court life and her unfulfilling marriage.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Margaret Stewart's marriage solidified the crucial 'Auld Alliance' between Scotland and France, directly influencing the balance of power during the Hundred Years' War and providing France with vital military support. Her story also offers insight into the personal cost of dynastic politics for medieval royal women.
